name: Zimbabwean Ndebele
confidence_why: 7 independent first-hand sources agree (5 agree, 1 refine), none contradicts
sweep_summary: nort2795 (Zimbabwean Ndebele) is in the catalog as fixed-dominant (penult), resting on Elliott 1897 p. xi. The two works with stress in the title are dead ends for word stress: Pietraszko 2016 turned out to be a WCCFL 34 handout/poster (downloaded from the author's site, saved) on disyllabic minimality as prosodically conditioned allomorphy, with no mention of stress, penult or lengthening; Greenhill 2016 is a JOSS Python-library paper wrongly attached to this languoid. Following the handout's references produced the real gain: Downing 2001 (SAL 30(1), open access, downloaded and saved) states first-hand that 'Ndebele words are, in fact, stressed on the penultimate syllable (this is indicated by lengthening the penult vowel)' (p. 37), with PhWord as the stress domain (p. 38) and penult length as the correlate of word stress (p. 40). This confirms the catalog's classification and should replace the 1897 one-liner as the deciding source, alongside Rycroft 1980 p. 112 (re-read held by the project; utterance-penult lengthening plus a hedged root-initial dynamic-stress caution). Also downloaded and read: Pietraszko's NLLT 2018 preprint (Ndebele content is tone spread and minimality; the penultimate-stress passage is about Swahili) and her 2017 dissertation (syntax, silent). Still unread: Rycroft 1983 BSOAS (paywalled at Cambridge Core, Unpaywall closed, no repository copy; priority high) and O'Neil 1913 (no digitized copy located; priority medium).org advancedsearch, the SAL journal site and the author's site directly.

new_statements.quote: As we can see in the data in (2), Ndebele words are, in fact, stressed on the penultimate syllable (this is indicated by lengthening the penult vowel), as is typical in Southern Bantu languages [Doke 1954; Myers 1987]. It is plausible to propose that in Ndebele, too, the minimality requirement on PhWords falls out from a requirement that they dominate a bisyllabic foot.
new_statements.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2001. Ungeneralizable minimality in Ndebele. Studies in African Linguistics 30(1): 33-58.
new_statements.locator: p. 37, sec. 3 (imperatives), sentence following ex. (2); corroborated p. 34 sec. 2.1, p. 38, p. 40
new_statements.reading: A first-hand, word-level statement by a Bantu phonologist working from her own 2000 Harare field data: word stress is fixed on the penultimate syllable of the phonological word and is realized as penult vowel length ('penult length is the correlate of stress assignment to the word in Ndebele', p. 40; 'penultimate syllables are always lengthened', p. 34). This is exactly the catalog's fixed-dominant penult coding, stated for Zimbabwean Ndebele alone (not jointly with Shona) and at the word rather than utterance level. It confirms the classification and is a better deciding source than Elliott 1897 p. xi (an 1897 joint Tebele/Shuna alphabet note); it also complements Rycroft 1980 p. 112, whose 3.1 frames penult length as an utterance-terminal marker.

audit.reasoning: The fixed: penultimate syllable coding rests on one sentence in an 1897 LMS missionary dictionary's alphabet note, stated jointly for 'Tebele and Shuna', graded snippet-reconstruction, with no copy. I downloaded that source and the quote is verbatim at p. xi, so nothing is fabricated. Every later source opened agrees that the penultimate syllable carries the prominence, realized as lengthening and most marked utterance/phrase-finally: Rycroft 1980 p. 112 (imposed penultimate length identical to Zulu), Sibanda 2004 p. 219 n. 2 (penult long by default), Downing 1990 p. 310 (penult lengthened 'due to regular stress on that syllable'), Doke 1967:94 via Hyman 2013 (stress in Nguni incl. Ndebele normally penultimate and long), Hyman 2013 Table 1 (Ndebele PL in all utterance types). So the penultimate stress is not at risk. sources.quote: p. 37: 'As we can see in the data in (2), Ndebele words are, in fact, stressed on the penultimate syllable (this is indicated by lengthening the penult vowel), as is typical in Southern Bantu languages [Doke 1954; Myers 1987].' p. 34: 'a colon following a vowel indicates length. (As will be discussed in more detail below, penultimate syllables are always lengthened.)' p. 38: 'Since PhWord is the domain for stress assignment in Ndebele, the minimality requirement on imperatives falls out from the requirement that PhWord dominate a stress foot.' p. 40: 'penult length is the correlate of stress assignment to the word in Ndebele. Normally, we do not expect to find more than one long vowel per word.'
sources.locator: p. 34 sec. 2.1; p. 37 sec. 3 (after ex. 2); p. 38; p. 40
sources.note: First-hand (data collected by the author at the University of Zimbabwe, Harare, May-July 2000, per fn. *): word stress is on the penultimate syllable, realized as penult vowel lengthening; the phonological word is the stress domain, one long (stressed) penult per PhWord, so a second long vowel diagnoses a second PhWord (e.g. [ba:za][ku:pha] 'they will give', p. 40 ex. 6a). Fixed penultimate, word-level.

[Glottolog ref 666497; Glottolog labels it grammar sketch by computer assignment; the Glottolog record itself says howpublished = Presentation given at WCCFL 34, cited in Pietraszko 2023 Glossa 8(1), DOI 10.16995/glossa.5849]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: Ndebele1 verbs exhibit morphological alternations sensitive to disyllabic minimality. [...] Under the standard assumption that prosodic words dominate a foot in the Prosodic Hierarchy (Nespor & Vogel, 1986; Selkirk, 1986), disyllabic minimality falls out as a well-formedness condition on PWords [...] Proposal: Minimality effects in Ndebele verbs are an instance of Prosodically Conditioned Allomorphy (PrCA).
sources.locator: handout p. 1, sec. 1 Introduction and Proposal
sources.note: Nothing. The handout and poster are about disyllabic minimality (yi-/si-/i- epenthesis in imperatives, participles, passives) analysed as prosodically conditioned allomorphy with a MinFoot constraint; the words stress, penult(imate), length(ening), accent and prominence do not occur anywhere in either text (a full-text search for stress/accent over the full extracted text output). It does not state where word stress falls.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: fn. 18 (p. 31): 'The penultultimate syllable may also be metrically strong and targeted by metrical tone spread, instead of the antipenult. The determination of which syllable in metrically strong depends on the so called conjoint/disjoint alternation, and it is immaterial to the present discussion. In disjoint forms, such as (68a), metrical spread always targets the antipenult.'
sources.note: The only Ndebele 'stress' content is metrical tone spread (H spreads to the antepenult, or the penult in conjoint forms) and disyllabic PWord minimality; the explicit penultimate-stress discussion (sec. 4, ex. 23-24) is about Swahili, not Ndebele. No statement of Ndebele word-stress placement or penultimate lengthening.
